[[File:Maximally matchable edges.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|A graph with its '''maximally matchable edges''' colored red. Including either of the gray edges in a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] prevents it from being [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum]].]]

In [[graph theory]], a '''maximally matchable edge''' in a graph is an edge that is included in at least one [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum-cardinality matching]] in the graph.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Tassa|first=Tamir|date=2012-03-16|title=Finding all maximally-matchable edges in a bipartite graph|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=423|pages=50–58|doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2011.12.071|issn=0304-3975|doi-access=free}}</ref> An alternative term is '''allowed edge'''.<ref name="DCC">{{Cite journal|last=De Carvalho|first=Marcelo H.|last2=Cheriyan|first2=Joseph|date=2005-10-01|title=An <math>O(VE)</math> algorithm for ear decompositions of matching-covered graphs|journal=ACM Transactions on Algorithms|volume=1|issue=2|pages=324–337|doi=10.1145/1103963.1103969|issn=1549-6325}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Matching Theory|last=Lovász|first=László|last2=Plummer|first2=Michael|date=2009-08-18|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=9780821847596|location=Providence, Rhode Island|doi = 10.1090/chel/367}}</ref>

A fundamental problem in [[Matching (graph theory)|matching theory]] is: given a graph ''G'', find the set of all maximally matchable edges in ''G.'' This is equivalent to finding the union of ''all'' maximum matchings in ''G'' (this is different than the simpler problem of finding a ''single'' maximum matching in ''G''). Several algorithms for this problem are known.

== Motivation ==
Consider a [[matchmaking]] agency with a pool of men and women. Given the preferences of the candidates, the agency constructs a [[bipartite graph]] where there is an edge between a man and a woman if they are compatible. The ultimate goal of the agency is to create as many compatible couples as possible, i.e., find a [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum-cardinality matching]] in this graph. Towards this goal, the agency first chooses an edge in the graph, and suggests to the man and woman on both ends of the edge to meet. Now, the agency must take care to only choose a maximally matchable edge. This is because, if it chooses a non-maximally matchable edge, it may get stuck with an edge that cannot be completed to a maximum-cardinality matching.<ref name=":0" />

== Definition ==
Let ''G'' = (''V'',''E'') be a graph, where ''V'' are the vertices and ''E'' are the edges. A ''matching'' in ''G'' is a subset ''M'' of ''E'', such that each vertex in ''V'' is adjacent to at most a single edge in ''M''. A ''maximum matching'' is a matching of maximum cardinality.

An edge ''e'' in ''E'' is called '''maximally matchable''' (or '''allowed''') if there exists a maximum matching ''M'' that contains ''e''.

== Algorithms for general graphs ==
Currently, the best known [[deterministic algorithm]] for general graphs runs in time <math>O(VE)</math> .<ref name=DCC/>

There is a [[randomized algorithm]] for general graphs in time <math>\tilde{O}(V^{2.376}) </math> .<ref name=":2">{{cite journal|last1=Rabin|first1=Michael O.|title=Maximum matchings in general graphs through randomization|url=http://www.eecs.umich.edu/%7Epettie/matching/Rabin-Vazirani-randomized-maximum-matching.pdf|journal=Journal of Algorithms|volume=10|issue=4|pages=557–567|year=1989|doi=10.1016/0196-6774(89)90005-9|last2=Vazirani|first2=Vijay V.}}.</ref> 

== Algorithms for bipartite graphs ==

* 
* 

In bipartite graphs, if a single [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum-cardinality matching]] is known, it is possible to find all maximally matchable edges in linear time -  <math>O(V+E)</math>.<ref name=":0" />

If a maximum matching is not known, it can be found by existing algorithms. In this case, the resulting overall runtime is <math>O(V^{1/2}E)</math> for general bipartite graphs and <math>O((V/\log V)^{1/2}E)</math> for dense bipartite graphs with <math>E=\Theta(V^2)</math>.

=== Bipartite graphs with a perfect matching ===
The algorithm for finding maximally matchable edges is simpler when the graph admits a [[perfect matching]].<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|sub.2.1}}

Let the bipartite graph be <math>G=(X+Y, E)</math>, where <math>X = (x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> and <math>Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)</math>. Let the perfect matching be <math>M = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\}</math>.

''Theorem:'' an edge ''e'' is maximally matchable if-and-only-if ''e'' is included in some ''M-alternating cycle'' - a cycle that alternates between edges in ''M'' and edges not in ''M''. ''Proof'':

* If ''e'' is in an alternating cycle, then either ''e'' is in ''M'', or - by inverting the cycle - we get a new perfect matching that contains ''e''. Hence, ''e'' is maximally matchable.
* Conversely, if ''e'' is maximally matchable, then it is in some perfect matching ''N''. By taking the [[symmetric difference]] of M and N, we can construct an alternating cycle that contains ''e''.

Now, consider a directed graph <math>H=(Z, E)</math>, where <math>Z = (z_1,\ldots,z_n)</math> and there is an edge from <math>z_i</math> to <math>z_j</math> in ''H'' iff <math>i\neq j</math> and there is an edge between <math>x_i</math> and <math>y_j</math> in ''G'' (note that by assumption such edges are not in ''M''). Each ''M''-alternating cycle in ''G'' corresponds to a ''[[directed cycle]]'' in ''H''.  A directed edge belongs to a directed cycle iff both its endpoints belong to the same [[strongly connected component]]. There are algorithms for finding all strongly connected components in linear time. Therefore, the set of all maximally matchable edges can be found as follows:

* Given the undirected bipartite graph <math>G=(X+Y, E)</math> and the perfect matching ''M'', mark every edge ''<math>(x_i,y_i)</math>'' in ''M'' as maximally matchable.
* Construct the directed graph <math>H=(Z, E)</math> as above.
* Find all strongly connected components in ''H''.
* For each ''i'', ''j'' such that ''<math>(z_i,z_j)</math>'' are in the same component, mark the edge ''<math>(x_i,y_j)</math>'' as maximally matchable.
* Mark all remaining edges as not maximally matchable.

=== Bipartite graphs without a perfect matching ===
Let the bipartite graph be <math>G=(X+Y, E)</math>, where <math>X = (x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> and <math>Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{n'})</math> and <math>n\leq n'</math>. Let the given maximum matching be <math>M = \{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_t,y_t)\}</math>, where <math>t \leq n \leq n'</math>. The edges in ''E'' can be categorized into two classes:

* Edges with both endpoints saturated by ''M''. We call such edges ''M-upper''.
* Edges with exactly one endpoint saturated by ''M''. We call such edges ''M-lower''.
* Note that there are no edges with both endpoints unsaturated by ''M'', since this would contradict the maximality of ''M''.

''Theorem:'' All <math>M</math>-lower edges are maximally matchable.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|sub.2.2}} ''Proof'': suppose <math> e = (x_i,y_j)</math> where <math>x_i </math> is saturated and <math>y_i </math> is not. Then, removing <math> e = (x_i,y_j)</math> from <math>M</math> and adding <math> e = (x_i,y_j)</math> yields a new maximum-cardinality matching.

Hence, it remains to find the maximally matchable edges among the ''M''-upper ones. 

Let ''H'' be the subgraph of ''G'' induced by the ''M''-saturated nodes. Note that ''M'' is a perfect matching in ''H''. Hence, using the algorithm of the previous subsection, it is possible to find all edges that are maximally matchable in ''H''. Tassa<ref name=":0" /> explains how to find the remaining maximally matchable edges, as well as how to dynamically update the set of maximally matchable edges when the graph changes.
